note: Yawl: a sailboat with two masts, the shorter one at the back.
The rising tide had begun to flow in from the sea.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Flood and flood-tide”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Bound down the river: heading downstream toward the sea.
The Thames is the chief river of England. It flows east through London to the North Sea; the sea-reach is its widest, lowest stretch.
Interminable: seeming to go on forever, without an end.
In the offing: out toward the open sea, beyond where ships anchor.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Offing”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Welded: joined so firmly that no seam shows.
Sprits: poles that stretch the top corner of a barge’s sail.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Sprit”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Gravesend is a river port in Kent on the south bank of the Thames, about 22 miles east of London.
Brooding: hanging over in a heavy, dark, threatening way.

anchor: biggest, and the greatest, town on earth
note: The town is London, the capital of Britain and of its worldwide empire, built along the Thames.
Luminous: giving off light, bright and glowing.
Yarns: long tales, often of adventure, told by sailors.
Bones: here, the pieces of the game of dominoes, which he stacks like a building.
Mizzen-mast: the mast nearest the stern of a sailing ship.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Mizen-mast”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Ascetic: strict and plain, like someone who denies himself comforts.
Pacifically: in a peaceful, calm way.
Benign: kindly, gentle, and harmless.
Essex is an eastern county of England, lying north of the Thames, with the North Sea on its east side.
Gauzy: thin and see-through, like fine cloth.
Diaphanous: so thin and light that you can see through it.
Imperceptible: so slight or slow that it cannot be noticed.
Forthwith: at once, without any delay.
Unruffled: smooth and calm, not disturbed in any way.
Venerable: deserving great respect because of its age.
August: grand, dignified, and impressive.
Abiding: lasting for a very long time, enduring.
Followed the sea: worked as a sailor.
Drake was an English sea captain who sailed around the world, setting out in 1577. Queen Elizabeth I knighted him aboard his ship.
Franklin (1786–1847) was an English naval officer and explorer. In 1845 he sailed to find a sea route across the Arctic, and he never returned.
Knights-errant: knights who wandered in search of adventure. Here, great sea adventurers.
The Golden Hind was Drake’s ship. Queen Elizabeth went aboard her at Deptford to knight him, and the ship was kept as a monument.
Rotund: round and plump. Flanks: the sides of a body, here of a ship.
Erebus and Terror were the ships of Franklin’s last expedition, with 129 officers and men. A whaler last saw them in July 1845.

anchor: from Deptford, from Greenwich, from Erith
note: Deptford, Greenwich, and Erith are towns on the Thames below London, where ships were built, fitted out, and sent to sea.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Deptford”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Deptford; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Greenwich”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Greenwich; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Erith”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Erith

note: ’Change: short for the Exchange, the market where merchants met.
Interlopers were traders who sailed to the East without the East India Company’s licence, breaking its monopoly.
Commonwealths: nations or states, ruled for the good of all their people.

anchor: Lights of ships moved in the fairway
note: Fairway: the navigable channel where ships pass up and down a river.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Fair-way”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Lurid: harsh, glowing, and unnatural.
Sedentary: spent mostly sitting, staying in one place.

anchor: In the immutability of their surroundings
note: Immutability: the state of never changing.
Disdainful: full of scorn for what one thinks unworthy.
Inscrutable: impossible to read or understand.
Spree: a short, lively outing of fun and drink.
Propensity: a natural tendency to do something.

anchor: the Romans first came here, nineteen hundred years ago
note: Rome’s conquest of Britain was undertaken by the emperor Claudius in AD 43. Marlow’s “nineteen hundred years” is a round figure.
Trireme: an ancient warship with three banks of oars.
Gaul was the Roman name for the lands of the Celtic peoples, mostly what is now France. Rome conquered it, and Caesar wrote an account of the war.
Legionaries: soldiers of the Roman legions.
Concertina: a small folding instrument squeezed in and out to make music. Here it means a ship that bends.
Falernian: a famous wine of ancient Rome.
Skulking: lurking out of sight, up to no good.
Ravenna is a city in northeast Italy. The emperor Augustus chose it as the base of a Roman fleet.
Toga: the loose outer robe worn by a Roman citizen.
Prefect: a high Roman official in charge of a district.

anchor: the pose of a Buddha preaching
note: The Buddha was the Indian religious teacher on whose teachings Buddhism is founded. Marlow, sitting cross-legged with palm raised, is compared to him.

anchor: their administration was merely a squeeze
note: Squeeze: money forced out of people by those in power.
Tackle: to take on a hard job and try to deal with it.
Redeems: makes up for faults and saves from being bad.
Fresh-water sailor: one who sails rivers and lakes, not the open sea.
Loafing: wasting time, doing nothing useful.
Hankering: a strong, restless wish.
The river is the Congo. Conrad wrote in A Personal Record that as a boy he put his finger on the blank map of Africa and later went there.
source: Joseph Conrad, A Personal Record (1912), https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/687; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Congo”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Congo

anchor: a Company for trade on that river
note: In 1885 Leopold II, King of the Belgians, became head of the Congo Free State. Trading companies bought its ivory and rubber.
Fleet Street is a street in London long known for its newspapers and printing; its name also meant the London press.
Continental: from mainland Europe, not Britain.
By hook or by crook: by any means at all.
Personage: a person of rank and importance.
Skipper: the captain of a ship.
Scuffle: a short, rough, confused fight.
Thunderstruck: astonished, as if hit by lightning.
Tentative: hesitant, not yet sure of itself.
Calamities: terrible disasters that bring great suffering.
Stepped into his shoes: took over his job.
Askew: crooked, turned to one side.
The Channel is the English Channel, the narrow sea between England and France. Crossing it takes Marlow from Britain to the Continent.
From the Bible: Jesus calls hypocrites “whited sepulchres,” tombs painted white outside but “full of dead men’s bones” within.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Matthew 23:27, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

note: Venetian blinds: window blinds made of slats that can be tilted.
Somnambulist: a person who walks in their sleep.
Deal: pine or fir wood.
Deuce: a mild word for the devil, used for emphasis. A deuce of a lot means a great deal.
Lager-beer: beer brewed cool and slowly fermented, as in Germany.
Compassionate: showing pity and kindness for someone’s trouble.
Sanctuary: here, a private inner room. The word first meant a holy place.
Frock-coat: a man’s long, formal coat that reaches the knees.
Bon voyage: French for “have a good trip.”
Ominous: giving a sense that something bad will happen.
Feverishly: in a hot, hurried, restless way.
Foot-warmer: a box or stool that holds hot coals or water to warm the feet.

anchor: a cat reposed on her lap
note: Reposed: lay at rest, resting quietly.
Placidity: calm, with no sign of worry or feeling.
Countenances: faces, or the expressions on them.
Eerie: strange and frightening in a way that gives chills.
Uncanny: strange in a way that seems unnatural. Fateful: seeming settled by destiny.
Pall: a heavy cloth spread over a coffin.
Latin for “hail.” The next line is the Latin salute of fighters before a staged battle: “We who are about to die salute you.”
Latin: “those about to die salute you.” In Suetonius, fighters in a staged sea battle gave this salute to Emperor Claudius.
source: Suetonius, Lives of the Twelve Caesars, Claudius 21, trans. A. Thomson, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/6400

anchor: a young chap wearing his hat over the left eyebrow
note: Chap: a fellow, a man.
Cravat: a man’s neck-cloth, a kind of necktie.
Joviality: cheerful, hearty good humor.
Vermouth: a wine flavoured with herbs, often drunk before a meal.
Quoth: said (an old word).
Sententiously: in a pompous, preachy way.
Calipers: a tool with two curved legs for measuring thickness or distance.
Gaberdine: a long, loose outer coat.

anchor: the crania of those going out there
note: Crania: skulls, the bones of the head.
Alienist: an old word for a doctor who treats mental illness.
Imperturbably: in a way that nothing can upset.
Messieurs: French for “gentlemen,” the plural of monsieur.
Dependency: a country ruled by another country.
Erroneous: wrong, containing a mistake.
Adieu: French for “goodbye,” said when parting.
Dignitary: a person who holds a high position.
Two-penny-half-penny: cheap, petty, of little worth.
Emissary: a person sent out on a mission for someone.
Apostle: one of Jesus’s first twelve followers, sent out to spread his teaching. Here, a missionary for a cause.
Humbug: nonsense, fake talk meant to fool.

anchor: the labourer is worthy of his hire
note: From the Bible: Jesus tells his followers that “the labourer is worthy of his hire,” meaning a worker deserves his pay.
source: The Bible (King James Version), Luke 10:7, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/10

note: Imposter: a person who pretends to be someone he is not. Marlow means he felt like a fraud.
Enigma: a puzzle, a thing hard to understand.
Insipid: dull, with no flavor or interest.
Grimness: a stern, forbidding look.

anchor: The edge of a colossal jungle
note: Colossal: huge, enormous, of vast size.
Levy toll: collect a tax or fee by authority.
Grand Bassam was a port in the French colony of Ivory Coast. Little Popo was a coastal town in Togoland, a German colony. Both lie on the West African coast.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Ivory Coast”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Ivory_Coast; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Togoland”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Togoland

note: Sordid: dirty and low. Farce: a silly comedy full of absurd events.
Back-cloth: the painted cloth hung at the back of a stage.
Delusion: a false belief or idea.
Grotesque: strangely and oddly shaped, almost absurd.
Man-of-war: a ship armed for war, a warship.
Ensign: the flag a ship flies to show her nation.
Projectile: an object fired or thrown, here a shell.
Lugubrious: gloomy and mournful. Drollery: odd, dark humor.
Dissipated: scattered and driven away.
Catacomb: an underground burial place with passages and tombs.
Mangroves: tropical trees that grow in muddy salt water on tangled roots.
Impotent: powerless, unable to act.
Particularized: clear in its details, not general.

anchor: We anchored off the seat of the government
note: The seat of government was Boma, a port on the north bank of the Congo about 60 miles from its mouth.

anchor: a place thirty miles higher up
note: This is Matadi, the highest point on the lower Congo that sea-going ships can reach. Cataracts stretching about 60 miles block the river above it.
source: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Congo Free State”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Congo_Free_State; Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th ed. (1911), “Congo”, https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica/Congo

note: Morose: sullen, gloomy, and unwilling to talk.
Athwart: across, from one side to the other.
Vigilantly: watching carefully for danger.

anchor: At last we opened a reach
note: Opened a reach: came in sight of a straight stretch of river.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Reach, or ratch”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Excavations: holes dug in the ground.
Declivity: a slope that goes downward, a hillside.
Devastation: ruin, great and widespread destruction.

anchor: A jetty projected into the river
note: Jetty: a landing wharf built out into the water.
Recrudescence: a new outbreak after a pause.
Railway-truck: a small open wagon that runs on rails.
Detonation: a sudden, loud explosion.
Objectless: having no aim or purpose.
Loins: the hips and lower part of the body.
Bights: the loops or slack curves of a rope or chain.
source: W. H. Smyth, The Sailor’s Word-Book (1867), “Bight”, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/26000

note: Insoluble: impossible to solve or explain.
Meagre: thin and scanty, lacking flesh.
Dilated: stretched wide open, made larger.
Despondently: in a hopeless, downhearted way.

anchor: hoisted his weapon to his shoulder with alacrity
note: Alacrity: quick, cheerful, eager readiness to act.
Rascally: mischievous and a little dishonest.
Lusty: full of vigor and strength.
Flabby: soft and limp, without strength.
Rapacious: greedy, grasping for whatever can be taken.
Insidious: harmful in a sly, gradual way that is hard to notice.
Obliquely: at a slant, not straight.
Philanthropic: aimed at helping people.
Wanton: senseless and cruel, done for no reason.
The Inferno is the first part of Dante’s poem the Divine Comedy, a journey down through the circles of hell. Here it means a place like hell.

anchor: half effaced within the dim light
note: Effaced: rubbed out, hard to see.
Legality: the quality of being lawful.
Uncongenial: unpleasant, not suited to one’s needs.
Moribund: close to death, dying.
Worsted: a smooth woollen yarn.
Propitiatory: meant to win the favor of a spirit or god.
Pestilence: a deadly, fast-spreading disease.
Alpaca: a thin, light cloth made of alpaca wool.
Indissolubly: in a way that cannot be broken or undone.
Dummy: a model of a human figure used to show clothes.

anchor: the great demoralization of the land
note: Demoralization: loss of spirit, discipline, and good conduct.
Linen: here, shirts and collars made of linen cloth. Sport: to wear proudly.
Apple-pie order: perfectly neat and in place.
Rubbishy: cheap, worthless, of poor quality.
Ivory, from elephant tusks, was a main export of the Congo. With rubber, it made the Congo Free State rich enough to pay its way.
Truckle-bed: a low bed on small wheels, kept under another bed.
Clerical errors: mistakes in writing or copying figures and records.
Elicited: drew out, got by asking.
Caravan: a long line of people carrying goods and traveling together.
Uncouth: strange, rough, and not refined.
Lamentable: sad and pitiful, deserving regret.
Composure: calm self-control, a steady and untroubled manner.

anchor: alluding with a toss of the head
note: Alluding: referring to something without naming it.
Tumult: a loud, confused uproar.
Insensible: unconscious, not able to feel or notice anything.

anchor: through thickets, down and up chilly ravines
note: Thickets: dense clumps of bushes. Ravines: deep, narrow valleys.
Yokels: country people, seen as simple and unschooled.
Pathetically: in a way that stirs pity.
Water-gourd: a dried hard-shelled fruit used as a water bottle.
Zanzibaris are people from Zanzibar, a sultanate on islands off East Africa that Britain protected. Here they are an armed escort for a white agent.
Exasperating: extremely irritating, enough to make one lose patience.

anchor: carried in a hammock slung under a pole
note: Hammock: a hanging bed of canvas or netting, here carried between bearers on a pole.
Stone: a British weight of 14 pounds. Sixteen stone is 224 pounds.
Jibbed: refused to go on, like a balking horse.
Sneaked: slipped away secretly, trying not to be seen.
Mutiny: a revolt against those in charge.
Hobbled: walked with difficulty and a limp.
Scrub: low, stunted bushes and brush.
Crazy: here, shaky and about to fall. Rushes: tall water plants with hollow stems.
Languidly: slowly and without energy.
Volubility: a fast, smooth flow of talk.
Digressions: wanderings away from the main subject.

anchor: trenchant and heavy as an axe
note: Trenchant: sharp and cutting, like a blade.
Indefinable: impossible to describe exactly.
Stealthy: secret and sly, meant not to be noticed.

anchor: no genius for organizing, for initiative
note: Initiative: the ability to start things without being told.

anchor: the deplorable state of the station
note: Deplorable: shameful and very bad.
Rout: a complete collapse. Constitutions: here, bodily health.
Pompously: in a showy, self-important way.
Externals: outward appearances, how things look from outside.

anchor: Men who come out here should have no entrails
note: Entrails: the inner organs, the guts.

anchor: quarrels of the white men about precedence
note: Precedence: the right to come first, according to rank.
Insolence: rude, scornful disrespect toward others.
Sealing-wax: wax melted and pressed on a letter to close it.
Jeopardy: danger of loss or harm.
Dumfounded: struck speechless with surprise.
Verandah: a roofed porch along the side of a house.
Nicety: careful, exact attention to detail.
Requisite: needed for a purpose, necessary.
Pilgrims: Marlow’s mocking name for the white agents, who carry long staves like pilgrims.
Rapacity: greed that grabs whatever it can.
Invincible: too strong to be beaten.
Calico: cheap, printed cotton cloth.
Avenging: punishing a wrong, getting even.
Dismantled: taken apart, with its equipment removed.
Cutting capers: leaping about in a lively, playful way.
Embers: glowing bits of burning coal or wood.
Stand-offish: cold, keeping others at a distance.
Dressing-case: a small case holding combs, brushes, and razors.
Assegais: slender spears with iron tips, used in southern Africa.
Beguiled the time: made the hours pass pleasantly.
Back-biting: saying spiteful things about people who are not there.
Intriguing: secretly plotting, scheming against someone.

anchor: a way of looking at a halter
note: Halter: a rope or strap put around a horse’s head to lead it.
Pumping: here, questioning someone closely to get information.
Mica: a mineral that splits into thin, shiny sheets.
Superciliousness: cool, scornful pride that looks down on others.
Baffled: puzzled, kept from understanding.
Prevaricator: a person who avoids the truth, a liar.
Draped: dressed in loose, flowing cloth.
Prodigy: a person with an amazing, exceptional gift.
Declaim: to speak loudly and with show, as an orator does.
Listlessly: without energy or interest.
Indefatigable: never tired, able to keep going and going.
Transgression: breaking a rule or law, a wrongdoing.
Conflagrations: large, destructive fires that spread widely.
Crestfallen: sad and let down, dejected.
Servile: eager to please like a servant.
Muffs: clumsy, foolish people who bungle things.
Gesticulating: making lively gestures with the hands and arms.
Spectrally: like a ghost, pale and unreal.
Mephistopheles is the chief devil in the legend of Faust. Papier-mâché is molded paper pulp, so this devil is hollow and fake.
Precipitately: in a headlong rush, too fast.
Primeval: belonging to the earliest ages of the world.
Rank: here, growing too thick and wild.
Matted: tangled together in a thick mass.

anchor: while the man jabbered about himself
note: Jabbered: talked fast and foolishly.

anchor: an appeal or as a menace
note: Menace: a threat of harm.
Commingling: a blending of different things together.
Mangled: badly torn up and damaged.
Wantonly: recklessly, without any good reason or cause.

anchor: What I really wanted was rivets
note: Rivets: metal pins hammered through steel plates to join them. The steamboat needs them to mend its hull.
Ghastly: horrible, shocking. Glazed: given a shiny finish.
Confidential: ready to share secrets and private matters.
Unresponsive: not answering or reacting.
Dictation: words spoken aloud for another person to write down.

anchor: I stuck to my salvage night and day
note: Salvage: property saved from a wreck, here the raised steamer.

anchor: That animal has a charmed life
note: Charmed life: a life protected as if by magic from harm.
Apprehend: to grasp with the mind, to understand.
Curt: short and rude, abrupt.

anchor: the battered, twisted, ruined, tin-pot steamboat
note: Tin-pot: cheap and of poor quality.
Clambered: climbed awkwardly, using hands and feet.
Laze: to rest and do nothing.

anchor: rather chummed with the few mechanics
note: Chummed: became friendly with, like a pal.
Foreman: a worker in charge of a crew.
Boiler-maker: a worker who builds and repairs steam boilers.
Widower: a man whose wife has died.
Connoisseur: an expert who knows and enjoys the fine points of something.
Serviette: a table napkin, here used as a beard-wrap.

anchor: We capered on the iron deck
note: Capered: jumped and skipped about playfully.
Hulk: the body of an old ship, no longer fit for sailing.
Hovels: small, dirty, miserable huts for living in.
Exuberant: growing in rich, overflowing abundance.
Festoons: hanging loops or garlands of leaves and branches.
Ichthyosaurus: an extinct sea reptile shaped like a fish, from the age of the dinosaurs.
Infliction: a burden or punishment. Visitation: an unwelcome visit, like a plague.
Instalments: parts of a whole delivered one at a time.

anchor: with the loot of innumerable outfit shops
note: Loot: goods taken by force, stolen goods.
Equitable: fair and just to everyone concerned.
Inextricable: so tangled that it cannot be sorted out.
El Dorado, Spanish for “the gilded one,” first meant a South American king said to cover himself in gold dust, then a legendary golden city.
Buccaneers: pirates or sea robbers who prey on others.
Hardihood: firm courage, boldness in facing danger.
Audacity: daring, bold courage, often to the point of rudeness.

anchor: carried his fat paunch with ostentation
note: Ostentation: showy display meant to attract notice.
Infested: overran in large, troublesome numbers.
Confab: a casual talk, a chat.
